q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 applies DISTINCT in a subquery on (ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN) before joining with ITM, while Q2 applies DISTINCT after joining all three tables on (ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN). This can lead to different results if there are multiple ITP rows for the same ITEMN linking to PUR rows with the same VENDN, as the subquery in Q1 reduces duplicates early, potentially affecting the join with ITM. In contrast, Q2 may produce duplicate (ITEMN, VENDN) rows during the join that are later removed by DISTINCT, but the final output should be the same. However, a counterexample exists where an ITEMN in ITM has multiple ITP rows linking to PUR with the same VENDN, but one PUR row has ODATE>85 and another has ODATE<=85, causing Q1 to include the VENDN only once from the subquery, while Q2 might not include it at all if the join conditions filter it out, but in this case, they behave similarly. The key difference arises when there are ITEMN in ITP not in ITM or vice versa, but under the schema constraints, the output ITEMN must be in both ITM and ITP. A valid counterexample involves an ITEMN with multiple ITP rows linking to PUR with different VENDNs, where one VENDN is associated with ODATE>85 and another with ODATE<=85, but after filtering, both queries return the same set. To illustrate a difference, consider an ITEMN in ITM that has no ITP row, but in Q2, it might be included due to implicit cross-join behavior without proper conditions, but with the given WHERE clauses, it is excluded in both. Thus, for this schema, they are equivalent, but a counterexample can be constructed where the DISTINCT in Q1 causes a different set of VENDNs to be considered for the same ITEMN.
counterexample: INSERT INTO ITM (ITEMN, TYPE) VALUES (10, 1); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMN, PONUM) VALUES (10, 100); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMN, PONUM) VALUES (10, 101); INSERT INTO PUR (PONUM, ODATE, VENDN) VALUES (100, 90, 1); INSERT INTO PUR (PONUM, ODATE, VENDN) VALUES (101, 80, 1);
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes an ITEMN in ITM with multiple ITP rows linking to PUR rows with the same VENDN but different ODATE values. One PUR row has ODATE>85, and another has ODATE<=85. Both queries return the same result because the ODATE filter excludes the row with ODATE<=85, and DISTINCT ensures only unique (ITEMN, VENDN) pairs are output. To trigger a difference, consider an ITEMN in ITM that has an ITP row linking to a PUR row with ODATE>85 and VENDN X, and another ITP row linking to a PUR row with ODATE>85 and VENDN Y, but if VENDN X and Y are the same, DISTINCT in Q1 reduces it to one row early, while in Q2, it is reduced after the join, resulting in the same output. A true difference would require ITEMN not in both tables or null values, but under the schema, they are equivalent.

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 includes an additional condition Y.B = Z.B. In a database where R2 has duplicate A values (which violates the PRIMARY KEY constraint), this condition filters rows where Y and Z have different B values for the same A, while Q2 does not. Under the given schema with PRIMARY KEY on R2.A, Y.A = Z.A implies Y and Z are the same row, so Y.B = Z.B is always true, making the queries equivalent for any valid database. However, if duplicates were allowed, the results would differ.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R1 VALUES (1, 100); INSERT INTO R2 VALUES (1, 10); INSERT INTO R2 VALUES (1, 20);
counterexample_dsp: A test database where R2 contains two rows with the same A value but different B values, and R1 has a matching A. This causes Q1 to return only Z rows where Y.B = Z.B (each distinct B once), while Q2 returns all Z rows with matching A (including duplicates). Note that this violates the PRIMARY KEY constraint on R2.A.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent because both queries return the set of (NP, TYPE, ITEMNO) for each distinct (ITEMNO, NP) pair from ITP where NP > 1000 and ITEMNO exists in ITM. The DISTINCT in Q1 is applied before the join on ITP columns, and in Q2 after the join on all columns, but since ITM has a primary key on ITEMNO (ensuring unique ITEMNO and fixed TYPE per ITEMNO), the effective distinct is on (ITEMNO, NP) for both queries.
counterexample: INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 1100), (1, 1100); INSERT INTO ITM (ITEMNO, TYPE) VALUES (1, 10);
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists where Q1 and Q2 return different results under the given schema and constraints. However, for illustration, with data where ITP has duplicate rows for the same ITEMNO and NP, both queries output the same number of rows.

q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 applies DISTINCT to ITP before joining with ITM, which removes duplicate (ITEMNO, NP) pairs from ITP. Q2 joins ITP and ITM first and then applies DISTINCT to the result. The difference can occur when ITP has multiple rows with the same ITEMNO but different NP values; in such cases, Q1 ensures only distinct NP values per ITEMNO are considered before the join, while Q2 may include duplicate NP values for the same ITEMNO in the join result before applying DISTINCT. However, for the output set of (ITM.ITEMNO, NP), they are often the same, but a counterexample can highlight scenarios where the intermediate handling differs.
counterexample: INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 100); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 200); INSERT INTO ITM (ITEMNO, TYPE) VALUES (1, 1);
counterexample_dsp: ITP has multiple rows for the same ITEMNO with different NP values, and ITM has corresponding ITEMNO. For example, ITP has (1,100) and (1,200), and ITM has ITEMNO 1. Both queries output (1,100) and (1,200), so they are equivalent in this case. However, if ITP had duplicate (ITEMNO, NP) pairs, Q1 would remove them before the join, while Q2 would remove them after the join, but the final output remains the same. A true counterexample showing different results is not possible under the given schema and constraints, as the queries are semantically equivalent for all valid data.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0

counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the schema constraints as the queries are equivalent. However, if ITL had rows with ITEMN NULL and conditions true, both queries would not return any additional ITP rows due to NULL comparisons in SQL.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 returns distinct values of X.X from the join of A and B on YA=YB, while Q2 returns X.X from a self-join of A on X.X and join with B on YA=YB, which can produce duplicate rows if there are multiple rows in A with the same X value that satisfy the join condition with B. Since Q1 uses DISTINCT and Q2 does not, and the self-join in Q2 multiplies rows for the same X, the results can differ in the number of rows output for the same X values. The second part of Q2 (SELECT 1 AS AX FROM A X WHERE 1=0) always returns no rows and does not affect the difference.
counterexample: INSERT INTO A VALUES (1, 10); INSERT INTO A VALUES (1, 10); INSERT INTO B VALUES (10);
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes two rows in table A with the same X value (1) and the same YA value (10), and one row in table B with YB=10. This causes Q2 to output multiple rows for X=1 due to the self-join (specifically, 4 rows), while Q1 outputs only one distinct row for X=1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: Q1 checks for the existence of a row in R1 with X=1 that has a matching Y value in R2. Q2 additionally requires, through the self-join condition X.X = Y.X, that there is another row in R1 with the same X value (X=1), which may imply distinct rows in some interpretations. Thus, Q2 returns a result only if there are at least two rows in R1 with X=1 and at least one has a matching Y in R2, while Q1 requires only one such row.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R1 VALUES (1, 2); INSERT INTO R2 VALUES (2);

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 requires the condition A2 = A3 after ensuring A1 = A2, while Q2 requires A1 = A3 after ensuring A1 = A2. Although logically, if A1 = A2 is true, then A2 = A3 if and only if A1 = A3, making them equivalent in that case, the queries differ when A1 = A2 is false or unknown (due to NULL values). Specifically, when A1 = A2 is false, both queries exclude the row, but the conditions on A3 differ: Q1 checks A2 = A3, and Q2 checks A1 = A3. With NULL values, the evaluation of these conditions can lead to different truth values (e.g., one condition being unknown while the other is false), but in standard SQL, both queries will not select such rows, so they are equivalent for practical purposes. However, a counterexample can be constructed where the queries return different results if we consider a row where A1 = A2 is true, but A2 = A3 is true and A1 = A3 is false—though this is logically impossible, it highlights the theoretical difference in conditions.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R VALUES (1, 1, 2);
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes a row where A1 = 1, A2 = 1, and A3 = 2. For this row, Q1 does not select it because A2 = A3 is false (1 ≠ 2), while Q2 does not select it because A1 = A3 is false (1 ≠ 2). Thus, both queries return no rows for this data, showing they are equivalent in this case. However, to illustrate the difference in conditions, if it were possible for A1 = A2 to be true, A2 = A3 to be true, and A1 = A3 to be false, then Q1 would select the row and Q2 would not, but such a scenario is impossible due to logical transitivity.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent for the given schema because the cross join in Q1 does not alter the set of distinct values from R.X. The DISTINCT operator ensures that only unique values are returned, and since the cross join only repeats the values from R.X without introducing new ones, the result set is identical to that of Q2 for any instance of R.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists as Q1 and Q2 always return the same result for any data in R under the given schema. The cross join in Q1 merely duplicates the rows from R but does not change the distinct values when projecting only X.*.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Q1 uses a self-join with condition X.A = Y.A, which does not match NULL values due to SQL's three-valued logic (NULL = NULL is not true), so NULLs are excluded. Q2 directly selects distinct A values from R, including NULLs. Thus, when R contains NULL, Q1 omits it while Q2 includes it.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R VALUES (1); INSERT INTO R VALUES (NULL); INSERT INTO R VALUES (2);
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes rows with A values 1, NULL, and 2. The presence of NULL causes Q2 to return NULL in its result, but Q1 does not due to the join condition not matching NULL.

explanation: Q1 uses a self-join with an equality condition that filters out rows where A1 or A2 is NULL because NULL comparisons in SQL evaluate to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Q2 directly selects all distinct rows from R, including those with NULL values.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (1, 1); INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (NULL, 2);
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes one row with non-NULL values (1,1) and one row with a NULL value in A1 (NULL,2). Q1 returns only (1,1) due to the join condition excluding NULLs, while Q2 returns both (1,1) and (NULL,2).

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME

explanation: Q1 selects departments that have a course with the global maximum credits across all courses, while Q2 selects all departments that have at least one course by matching each department's maximum credit course. Thus, Q2 includes departments without the global maximum credit, whereas Q1 does not.
counterexample: INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 101, 1, 10); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 102, 2, 5);
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes two courses: one in department 1 with 10 credits (global maximum), and one in department 2 with 5 credits. Q1 returns only department 1, while Q2 returns both departments 1 and 2.
